q: Which explains why increasing the concentration of a solution increases the rate of reaction?
options: The particles become larger, so they collide more often
The particles move faster, so more have enough energy to react
The activation energy of the reaction is lower
There are more particles per unit volume, so collisions are more frequent
explain: A higher concentration puts more particles in each unit volume. The frequency of collisions rises and so does the rate.

q: Which is the best explanation of why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction?
options: The particles have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and more collisions have energy of at least Ea
The extra heat adds more reactant particles
The particles move faster but the number of collisions stays the same
The activation energy of the reaction becomes lower
explain: At a higher temperature particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent, and a greater proportion of them have energy of at least the activation energy.

q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
options: It increases the concentration of the reactants
It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
It increases the kinetic energy of the reactant particles
It raises the energy of the reactants above the activation energy
explain: A catalyst offers a different route with a lower Ea, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

q: What is meant by the activation energy, Ea, of a reaction?
options: The average kinetic energy of the particles in the mixture
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products
The total energy released when the reaction is complete
explain: Activation energy is the minimum collision energy needed to break bonds and start the reaction.

q: Why does a solid in powder form react faster than the same mass in large lumps?
options: The activation energy of the solid is lower
The particles of the solid have more kinetic energy
The solid has a higher concentration
More particles of the solid are exposed, so collisions with the other reactant happen more frequently
explain: Powdering increases the surface area. More solid particles are available to collide, so the collision frequency and the rate increase.

q: Which is the correct explanation of why increasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction increases its rate?
options: The activation energy of the reaction decreases
The gas particles are closer together, so there are more particles per unit volume and collisions are more frequent
The gas particles gain kinetic energy and move faster
The gas particles become smaller
explain: Raising the pressure compresses the gas, which increases the number of particles in a given volume and so the collision frequency.

q: Which statement about adding a catalyst to a reaction is correct?
options: The activation energy decreases but the energy of the reactants and products is unchanged
The mass of product formed is increased
The activation energy increases and the energy of the products decreases
The activation energy is unchanged and the energy of the products decreases
explain: A catalyst lowers Ea by giving an alternative pathway. It does not change the energies of reactants and products or the amount of product.

q: Which row is correct?
columns: Effect on proportion with energy ≥ Ea
options: Increasing surface area | collision frequency increases | proportion of particles with energy ≥ Ea increases
Increasing pressure of a gas | collision frequency decreases | proportion of particles with energy ≥ Ea stays the same
Increasing concentration | collision frequency increases | proportion of particles with energy ≥ Ea stays the same
Increasing temperature | collision frequency stays the same | proportion of particles with energy ≥ Ea increases
explain: Higher concentration only raises the collision frequency. Higher temperature raises both, and surface area and pressure changes do not affect the proportion of particles with enough energy.

q: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Why is the loss-in-mass method less suitable than collecting the gas in a syringe?
options: Hydrogen is very soluble in the acid
Hydrogen is so light that the loss in mass is too small to measure accurately
Hydrogen is heavier than the other products
Magnesium chloride gives off a gas as well
explain: Hydrogen has a very low relative formula mass so only a tiny mass is lost. Calcium carbonate with acid loses more mass as heavier carbon dioxide escapes.

q: Calcium carbonate reacts with dilute acid and the carbon dioxide is collected in an inverted measuring cylinder over water. Why is a gas syringe better?
options: Water would react with the calcium carbonate
A syringe makes the reaction faster
Carbon dioxide dissolves in water, so some gas would not be measured over water
Carbon dioxide reacts with the glass of the cylinder
explain: Carbon dioxide is soluble in water, which would make the measured volume too low. A gas syringe avoids this problem.

q: In a loss-in-mass experiment a loose plug of cotton wool is put in the neck of the flask. What is its purpose?
options: It stops the gas leaving the flask
It absorbs the carbon dioxide
It acts as a catalyst for the reaction
It stops acid spray leaving the flask but lets the gas escape
explain: Spray carried out with the gas would give a false loss in mass. The loose plug keeps liquid in while gas can still escape.

q: In a gas collection experiment, 36 cm³ is collected at 20 s and 60 cm³ at 60 s. What is the average rate between 20 s and 60 s?
options: 0.40 cm³/s
0.60 cm³/s
1.0 cm³/s
1.5 cm³/s
explain: Volume formed = 60 − 36 = 24 cm³ in 60 − 20 = 40 s. Rate = 24 ÷ 40 = 0.60 cm³/s.

q: Excess magnesium reacts with 25.0 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What is the maximum volume of hydrogen at room temperature and pressure? (1 mol of gas occupies 24 000 cm³)
options: 1.2 cm³
1200 cm³
600 cm³
300 cm³
explain: Moles of HCl = 0.0250 × 2.0 = 0.050 mol. Moles of H₂ = 0.050 ÷ 2 = 0.025 mol. Volume = 0.025 × 24 000 = 600 cm³.

q: A catalysed and an uncatalysed reaction use the same amounts of reactants. How do their gas-volume curves compare?
options: The catalysed curve levels off at a higher final volume
The catalysed curve is less steep but levels off at the same final volume
The catalysed curve is steeper but levels off at the same final volume
The curves are identical
explain: The catalyst increases the rate, so the curve is steeper, but the amount of reactant limits the final volume, which stays the same.

q: At room temperature most collisions between reactant particles do not lead to a reaction. What is the best reason?
options: The colliding particles do not have energy of at least the activation energy
The particles are too small to react
The particles are moving too fast to react
The particles collide too often
explain: A reaction occurs only if colliding particles have at least the activation energy. At low temperature few collisions meet this requirement.

q: Which symbol shows that a chemical reaction is reversible?
explain: The two-way arrow ⇌ shows that the reaction can go in both directions.

q: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals are heated gently in a test tube. What is observed?
options: There is no change
The crystals turn white and water droplets form on the cooler part of the tube
The crystals turn black and a gas that relights a glowing splint forms
The crystals turn from white to blue
explain: Heating drives off the water of crystallisation, leaving white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. The water condenses on the cooler glass.

q: A few drops of water are added to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. Which observation is correct?
options: It turns blue and becomes cooler
It turns blue and becomes warm
It turns pink and becomes warm
It stays white and dissolves to give a colourless solution
explain: The anhydrous solid combines with water to form blue hydrated crystals, and the reaction is exothermic so the solid warms up.

q: A piece of blue cobalt(II) chloride paper is dipped in water. What is observed?
options: It turns green
It turns pink
It turns white
It stays blue
explain: Water changes anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride from blue to pink, so the paper is used to test for water.

q: Which row gives the correct colours?
options: cobalt(II) chloride | blue | pink
copper(II) sulfate | white | blue
copper(II) sulfate | blue | pink
cobalt(II) chloride | pink | blue
explain: Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride is pink and the anhydrous form is blue. Hydrated copper(II) sulfate is blue and the anhydrous form is white.

q: Which equation represents a reversible reaction?
options: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)
2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)
CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(g)
explain: Only the hydration of copper(II) sulfate is shown with ⇌, because it can go in either direction depending on the conditions.

q: What is the result of a positive test for water using anhydrous copper(II) sulfate?
options: White powder turns pink
Blue crystals turn pink
White powder turns blue
Blue crystals turn white
explain: Water turns white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue.

q: What does the word hydrated mean in hydrated copper(II) sulfate?
options: The solid has been dissolved in water
The crystals contain water as part of their structure
The solid has water only on its surface
The solid has reacted with hydrogen
explain: A hydrated compound has water of crystallisation locked in its crystal structure.

q: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate has been heated until it is white. How can the blue colour be restored?
options: Place the white solid in a desiccator
Heat the white solid more strongly
Add sodium chloride to the white solid
Add water to the white solid
explain: The reaction is reversible. Adding water to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate forms the blue hydrated crystals again.

q: Which statement describes a reversible reaction?
options: All the reactants are used up and cannot be recovered
The reaction can only take place if a catalyst is present
The products can react to form the reactants again
The reaction takes place in only one direction
explain: In a reversible reaction the reaction can go forwards and backwards, so products can turn back into reactants.

q: A piece of cobalt(II) chloride paper has turned pink after testing a liquid. It is gently heated. What happens?
options: It stays pink
It turns white
It turns blue again
It turns black
explain: Heating removes the water, so the pink hydrated cobalt(II) chloride changes back to blue anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride.

q: A student heats 5.0 g of blue crystals of copper(II) sulfate and the mass falls. What is the best explanation?
options: The crystals dissolve in their own water
The sulfate decomposes to sulfur
Copper is lost as a vapour
Water is driven off, leaving anhydrous copper(II) sulfate
explain: The crystals lose their water of crystallisation as steam, so the solid becomes lighter and turns white.

q: What is the white solid left when blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated strongly?
options: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate
Copper(II) sulfide
Copper(II) oxide
Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate
explain: Gentle heating only removes the water. The white solid is copper(II) sulfate without water, which is called anhydrous.

q: What is the effect of heating hydrated cobalt(II) chloride crystals?
options: Pink crystals turn black
Blue crystals turn pink as water is lost
Pink crystals turn blue as water is lost
White crystals turn blue
explain: Heating drives off the water of crystallisation, changing pink hydrated cobalt(II) chloride into blue anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride.

q: Which statement describes a reversible reaction at equilibrium in a closed system?
options: The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
The forward reaction has stopped and the reverse reaction continues
All of the reactants have been converted into products
The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate and the concentrations stay constant
explain: At equilibrium both reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations do not change. They are constant but not necessarily equal.
